bio-eco-01-c3.text: NOAA National Ocean Service. What is eutrophication?. NOAA National Ocean Service.
bio-eco-01-c3.quote: Bacteria digest the dead plants, using up remaining oxygen, and giving off carbon dioxide.
bio-eco-01-c3.claim: Algal blooms follow, and when they decompose they use up the oxygen and kill fish.

bio-eco-02-c1.text: J. Michael Beman (2010). Energy Economics in Ecosystems. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-02-c1.quote: Vent communities are not supported by the heat coming out of these vents, but are instead sustained by the chemical compounds (e.g., methane and hydrogen sulphide) that are discharged from the vents and chemically converted by microorganisms, thereby generating energy.
bio-eco-02-c1.claim: Producers (autotrophs) capture energy: plants use photosynthesis; some bacteria use chemosynthesis (hydrothermal vents).

bio-eco-02-c2.text: Maciej Karpowicz, Irina Feniova, Michail I. Gladyshev, et al (2021). Transfer efficiency of carbon, nutrients, and polyunsaturated fatty acids in planktonic food webs under different environmental conditions. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-02-c2.quote: A major paradigm of ecology is that only about 10% of organic carbon production of one trophic level is incorporated into new biomass in the next trophic level (Lindeman, 1942).
bio-eco-02-c2.claim: On average, only about 10% of energy from one level is incorporated into the next: the rest is lost as heat through respiration.

bio-eco-02-c3.text: Brian R. Silliman, Christine Angelini (2012). Trophic Cascades Across Diverse Plant Ecosystems. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-02-c3.quote: Where sea otter populations have lingered, Estes & Duggins showed that they suppress the density and biomass of hold-fast grazing urchins and thus have a strong, indirect positive effect on the abundance of macroalgae (kelp).
bio-eco-02-c3.claim: The sea otter is a classic example: studies by James Estes and colleagues from the 1970s showed that sea otters control sea urchin populations, which in turn control kelp forests.

bio-eco-03-c1.text: Ocean acidification. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
bio-eco-03-c1.quote: During this time, the pH of surface ocean waters has fallen by 0.1 pH units. This might not sound like much, but the pH scale is logarithmic, so this change represents approximately a 30 percent increase in acidity.
bio-eco-03-c1.claim: Since the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped from ~8.2 to ~8.1: small in absolute terms but huge in chemical terms because pH is logarithmic.

bio-eco-03-c2.text: Anne Bernhard (2010). The Nitrogen Cycle: Processes, Players, and Human Impact. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-03-c2.quote: For example, root exudates from legume plants (e.g., peas, clover, soybeans) serve as a signal to certain species of Rhizobium, which are nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
bio-eco-03-c2.claim: Nitrogen fixation converts N2 into ammonia (NH3): done by specialised bacteria including Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes and free-living cyanobacteria.

bio-eco-04-c1.text: Charles Darwin (1872). The Origin of Species, Sixth Edition. Project Gutenberg.
bio-eco-04-c1.quote: if this be so, after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair.
bio-eco-04-c1.claim: Charles Darwin noted that even slow-breeding elephants could produce 19 million descendants in 750 years if all survived.

bio-eco-04-c2.text: Shandelle M. Henson, Robert A. Desharnais, Eric T. Funasaki, et al (2019). Predator-prey dynamics of bald eagles and glaucous-winged gulls at Protection Island, Washington, USA. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-04-c2.quote: In their classic paper on Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis) and snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus) populations, Elton and Nicholson (1942) used 100‐year records from the Hudson Bay Company on the numbers of pelts purchased from trappers.
bio-eco-04-c2.claim: The classic example: Canadian lynx and snowshoe hare data from Hudson's Bay Company fur records (1845–1935) show 10-year population cycles where hare peaks are followed by lynx peaks, then crashes.

bio-eco-04-c2.text: Shandelle M. Henson, Robert A. Desharnais, Eric T. Funasaki, et al (2019). Predator-prey dynamics of bald eagles and glaucous-winged gulls at Protection Island, Washington, USA. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-04-c2.quote: The classic predator–prey cycles of theoretical ecology (Figure 1a), often illustrated with lynx‐hare data, are produced by the Lotka–Volterra predator–prey ordinary differential equation model (Henson, 2012; Lotka, 1925; Volterra, 1926)
bio-eco-04-c2.claim: The Lotka-Volterra equations (developed independently in the 1920s) model these cycles mathematically.

bio-eco-05-c1.text: IPBES Secretariat (2016). Press Release: Pollinators Vital to Our Food Supply Under Threat. IPBES.
bio-eco-05-c1.quote: Between US$235 billion and US$577 billion worth of annual global food production relies on direct contributions by pollinators.
bio-eco-05-c1.claim: Biodiversity provides ecosystem services: pollination (worth ~$235 billion/year globally), water purification, climate regulation, soil formation, and medicines.

bio-eco-05-c2.text: Lily Linke, Christopher F. Clements (2024). A Sixth Mass Extinction? How Linguistic Uncertainty Shapes Our Understanding of the Biodiversity Crisis. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-05-c2.quote: Furthermore, the current rate of species extinction has been put between 100 and 1000 times the background rate across recent geological time
bio-eco-05-c2.claim: Current extinction rates are estimated at 100–1,000 times the background rate: driven by habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, and climate change.

bio-eco-05-c2.text: De Gao, Gad Perry (2016). Detecting the small island effect and nestedness of herpetofauna of the West Indies. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-05-c2.quote: The equilibrium theory of island biogeography (MacArthur and Wilson 1967), elaborating the relationship between immigration and the extinction of species to islands depending on their size and distance from the mainland
bio-eco-05-c2.claim: Island biogeography theory (MacArthur and Wilson, 1967) predicts that species number is a function of island area and isolation.

bio-eco-05-c3.text: (2024). World must act faster to protect 30% of the planet by 2030. Knowledge4Policy, European Commission.
bio-eco-05-c3.quote: The Protected Planet Report 2024 reveals that 17.6% of land and inland waters and 8.4% of the ocean and coastal areas globally are within documented protected and conserved areas.
bio-eco-05-c3.claim: Protected areas (national parks, marine reserves) cover ~17% of land and ~8% of ocean, but placement, management quality, and connectivity matter as much as coverage.

bio-eco-06-c1.text: Jennifer M. Lang, M. Eric Benbow (2013). Species Interactions and Competition. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-06-c1.quote: Commensalism is an interaction in which one individual benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed.
bio-eco-06-c1.claim: Predation (one eats the other), competition (both lose access to a resource), mutualism (both benefit: pollination, mycorrhizae), commensalism (one benefits, other unaffected), parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense without immediate killing).

bio-eco-06-c2.text: Monica M. Moritsch, Peter T. Raimondi (2018). Reduction and recovery of keystone predation pressure after disease-related mass mortality. Ecology and Evolution.
bio-eco-06-c2.quote: Experimental sea star removals in many locations on the Pacific coast have demonstrated that when P. ochraceus abundances are severely reduced for a sufficiently long duration, M. californianus increase in percent cover
bio-eco-06-c2.claim: Remove a keystone species and the community can transform dramatically.

bio-eco-06-c3.text: Jennifer M. Lang, M. Eric Benbow (2013). Species Interactions and Competition. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-06-c3.quote: Whether by interference or exploitation, over time a superior competitor can eliminate an inferior one from the area, resulting in competitive exclusion
bio-eco-06-c3.claim: The competitive exclusion principle (Gause): two species with identical niches can't coexist; one will outcompete the other.

bio-eco-06-c3.text: Jennifer M. Lang, M. Eric Benbow (2013). Species Interactions and Competition. Nature Education Knowledge (Scitable).
bio-eco-06-c3.quote: The outcomes of competition between two species can be predicted using equations, and one of the most well known is the Lotka-Volterra model (Volterra 1926, Lotka 1932).
bio-eco-06-c3.claim: The Lotka-Volterra equations formalize competition and predation dynamics: staples of theoretical ecology since the 1920s.

bio-eco-07-c1.text: Lisa Boström-Einarsson, Russell C. Babcock, Elisa Bayraktarov, et al (2020). Coral restoration: A systematic review of current methods, successes, failures and future directions. PLOS ONE.
bio-eco-07-c1.quote: defines restoration as “the process of assisting the recovery of an ecosystem that has been degraded, damaged, or destroyed”
bio-eco-07-c1.claim: Restoration aims to return a degraded ecosystem to a more natural state.

bio-eco-07-c3.text: Aurora Torres, Néstor Fernández, Sophus zu Ermgassen, et al (2018). Measuring rewilding progress. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B.
bio-eco-07-c3.quote: Rewilding is emerging as a promising restoration strategy to enhance the conservation status of biodiversity and promote self-regulating ecosystems while re-engaging people with nature.
bio-eco-07-c3.claim: Rewilding reintroduces ecosystem-engineering species (large herbivores, top predators) to restore self-regulating ecological dynamics.

bio-eco-08-c1.text: Xiaofan Wang, Xuhong Wang, Yun Li, et al (2024). Response of Extremely Small Populations to Climate Change: A Case of Trachycarpus nanus in Yunnan, China. Biology.
bio-eco-08-c1.quote: The distributions of species have recently shifted to a higher elevation at a median rate of 11.0 m per decade, and to a higher latitude at a median rate of 16.9 km per decade
bio-eco-08-c1.claim: Average range shift: ~17 km per decade poleward, ~11 m upslope per decade.

bio-eco-08-c1.text: Jian Liao, Zhenqi Wu, Haojie Wang, et al (2023). Projected Effects of Climate Change on Species Range of Pantala flavescens, a Wandering Glider Dragonfly. Biology.
bio-eco-08-c1.quote: A global-scale study revealed a significant trend of more than 1700 species migrating toward the poles, averaging 6.1 km/decade, and significant mean advancement of spring events by 2.3 days per decade
bio-eco-08-c1.claim: Phenological shifts: spring events (flowering, hatching, migration arrival) are happening earlier.

bio-eco-08-c2.text: Russell J. Schmitt, Sally J. Holbrook, Samantha L. Davis, et al (2019). Experimental support for alternative attractors on coral reefs. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
bio-eco-08-c2.quote: hysteresis existed in the herbivory–macroalgae relationship, creating the potential for coral–macroalgae bistability at some levels of herbivory
bio-eco-08-c2.claim: Tipping points are often hysteretic: even when conditions improve, the new state can persist.

bio-eco-08-c3.text: Shannon N. Rivera, Lucas Berio Fortini, Sheldon Plentovich, et al (2021). Perceived Barriers to the Use of Assisted Colonization for Climate Sensitive Species in the Hawaiian Islands. Environmental Management.
bio-eco-08-c3.quote: Assisted colonization is a translocation tool defined by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as the “intentional movement and release of an organism outside of its historical range”
bio-eco-08-c3.claim: Assisted migration, moving species ahead of climate shifts, is controversial but increasingly considered for endangered species.
